title: Confusion Matrix
tagline: A simple 2x2 table that shows exactly where your classifier is getting confused.
what_it_is: A confusion matrix is a table that compares your model's predictions to the actual true labels. For binary classification, it has four cells: True Positives (correctly predicted Yes), True Negatives (correctly predicted No), False Positives (predicted Yes but actually No – a 'false alarm'), and False Negatives (predicted No but actually Yes – a 'miss'). From these four numbers, you can calculate accuracy, precision, recall, and many other metrics. It tells you not just how many errors, but what kind of errors.
key_points: True Positive (TP): model said yes, actual yes. Hit.
True Negative (TN): model said no, actual no. Correct rejection.
False Positive (FP): model said yes, actual no. Type I error. False alarm.
False Negative (FN): model said no, actual yes. Type II error. Miss.
The sum of all four = total number of predictions.
why_it_exists: Accuracy alone hides critical information. A cancer test that always says 'no cancer' is 99% accurate if only 1% of people have cancer. But it misses every single cancer patient – a disaster. The confusion matrix exists because different errors have different costs. A false positive (telling a healthy person they have cancer) causes stress. A false negative (telling a sick person they are healthy) can kill. You need to see both separately. The confusion matrix gives you that view.
what_it_measures: The confusion matrix measures not just overall performance but the tradeoffs. From it you calculate precision: of all the times you said yes, how many were actually yes? Recall: of all the actual yes cases, how many did you catch? Specificity: of all actual no cases, how many did you correctly reject? False positive rate: of actual no cases, how many did you falsely say yes? Each number tells a different story about your model's behavior.
intuition: Imagine you are a security guard at an airport. Your job is to flag potential threats. Your model (the metal detector) can beep (predict threat) or not. Confusion matrix: True Positive: beep and actual weapon. True Negative: no beep and no weapon. False Positive: beep but no weapon (someone's belt buckle). False Negative: no beep but actual weapon (bad). The matrix lets you see: are you annoying innocent travelers (many false positives) or are you missing real threats (false negatives)? You cannot optimize both at the same time. The matrix makes this tradeoff explicit.
when_to_use: Always look at the confusion matrix for any classification problem. It is the first thing to check after training.
When you need to choose a threshold for your classifier. Vary the threshold and see how TP, FP, FN, TN change.
When costs of errors are different. For spam detection, a false positive (email marked spam that is important) is worse than a false negative (spam in inbox). You want low FP, even if FN increases.
When you want to explain model performance to non-technical people. The 2x2 grid is intuitive.
when_not_to_use: Do not use the confusion matrix as your only evaluation if you have more than two classes. For multiclass, use a larger matrix (k x k) but it gets messy. Use per-class metrics instead.
Do not use raw counts if your dataset is imbalanced. A confusion matrix with 1000 TNs and 10 TPs looks impressive, but the TP count is very low. Look at normalized percentages.
Do not forget to label which class is positive. The matrix is not symmetric. Swapping positive/negative swaps the cells.
common_mistakes: Confusing which cell is which. Remember: the row is actual, the column is predicted (or vice versa depending on library). In scikit-learn, rows = actual, columns = predicted. Always check the documentation.
Focusing only on total accuracy and ignoring the four cells. A 95% accurate model might have zero TP and still be 95% accurate if the class is rare.
Using the confusion matrix without normalizing. For imbalanced data, look at percentages per class (e.g., of all actual positives, what fraction were caught?).
Thinking a perfect confusion matrix means a perfect model. It might just mean your test set is too easy or your model memorized.
ds_usage: In Python: `from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix`. Run `cm = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred)`. This returns a 2D array. Plot it with `seaborn.heatmap(cm, annot=True)`. For multiclass, same function works. Use `normalize='true'` to get recall per class, or `normalize='pred'` to get precision per class. Also `ConfusionMatrixDisplay.from_estimator()` is a quick plot. Always look at the matrix before calculating any single-number metric.
